dedupe_keys.name: cospas sarsat satellite aided search and rescue system in operation

description: This emergency-response and operations case covers Cospas-Sarsat, the international satellite system that detects and locates distress beacons carried by aircraft, ships and people on land and passes the alerts to rescue coordination centres. Beacons transmit on 406 MHz; the signals are picked up by search and rescue payloads on satellites in low Earth orbit (LEOSAR), geostationary orbit (GEOSAR) and, increasingly, medium Earth orbit (MEOSAR) on GPS, Galileo and GLONASS satellites, and relayed to ground stations that compute the position. Reported figures give five LEOSAR, seven GEOSAR and more than 35 MEOSAR satellites in operation, rising to at least 75 satellites at full strength; the Galileo search and rescue payload was first switched on in January 2013. Programme statistics show that from September 1982 to December 2023 the system helped rescue at least 63,745 people in 19,883 events; in 2021, 2022 and 2023 it helped rescue 3,623, 3,223 and 3,109 people, and in 2024 its alerts assisted in 1,171 incidents with 3,211 people rescued, 42 per cent of events on land, 41 per cent at sea and 17 per cent in aviation. Coverage: global, 1982 onward. Format and access: programme status papers to ICAO, NOAA SARSAT pages and annual statistics, free. Caveats: figures count incidents where alert data assisted, not rescues caused by the system alone; detailed incident data are not public. Simulation uses: emergency response time and coverage of satellite alerting, reliance of rescue services on space infrastructure, and effects of losing satellite segments. Related records: Galileo's emergency warning service and the QZSS DC Report use navigation satellites for public warning.
